extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates / graduate students and researchers learning algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's Foundations of Algebraic Geometry)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for constructing and recognising line bundles (invertible sheaves) on projective schemes, identifying their global sections, and using sections/linear series to produce (and test) morphisms to projective space (including criteria for embeddings, degrees, and related constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Behaviour of ideal sheaves under pullback / right-exactness
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying µ* to the closed subscheme exact sequence is a priori only right-exact, so in general µ*IX/Y need not equal IX′/Y′; IX′/Y′ is the image of µ*IX/Y in OY′.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affined-locally, the ideal of the pullback is generated by the pullback of the ideal (see Exercise 10.2.B). In particular, equality µ*IX/Y = IX′/Y′ holds if µ is flat (Remark 14.5.8). Exercise 14.5.J gives a counterexample when µ is not flat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of a quasicoherent sheaf from a graded module (~ functor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a graded S-module M•, define a quasicoherent sheaf #M on Proj S by taking for each homogeneous f of positive degree the ((M_f))0 piece and gluing via the obvious restriction isomorphisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction produces a quasicoherent sheaf because it is quasicoherent on each distinguished open D(f) and the local pieces satisfy the cocycle conditions. The subscript 0 is the degree-0 graded piece. See Exercises 4.5.I, 2.5.E and 14.6.A for stalk and local descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exactness of the ~ functor
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Everything in the construction is exact, so short exact sequences of graded modules give short exact sequences of the associated quasicoherent sheaves (Exercise 14.6.B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-equivalence of categories: graded modules vs quasicoherent sheaves on Proj
rubrics_metrics.description: The functor ~ from graded S-modules to quasicoherent sheaves on Proj S is not an equivalence of categories in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 14.6.C and the following discussion: two graded modules that agree in high enough degrees can give isomorphic sheaves, so the map on isomorphism classes need not be bijective. For finitely-generated modules one may form a saturation/process (category C and limit description) to recover an equivalence with finite-type quasicoherent sheaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphism of graded modules induces morphism of sheaves (compatibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: A map φ : M• → N• of graded modules induces on D(f) the map ((M_f))0 → ((N_f))0, and these local maps commute with restriction, giving a global sheaf morphism #M → #N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the explicit way graded maps produce maps of quasicoherent sheaves on Proj; check commutative diagrams over overlaps D(fg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of O(m) on projective space via transition functions
rubrics_metrics.description: On P1 and more generally Pn, the invertible sheaf O(1) is defined by trivializations on standard affine patches with transition function xi/j = x_i/x_j (for O(1)); O(m) is defined using the m-th powers of those transition functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transition functions satisfy the cocycle condition. Negative m interpreted by duals/tensor inverses. Tensor rules: O(m) ⊗ O(m′) ≅ O(m + m′).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of global sections Γ(Pn, O(m)) with homogeneous degree-m polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: Global sections of O(m) on Pn are naturally identified with homogeneous polynomials of degree m in the projective coordinates (the degree-m part of the graded ring).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identification explains vanishing loci of sections, multiplication of sections (O(m) ⊗ O(n) → O(m+n)), and allows explicit dimension counts (Exercise 15.1.C and 15.1.A giving dim h0 results). The construction works over any ring A (Exercise 15.1.D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation by global sections ↔ base-point-free
rubrics_metrics.description: An invertible sheaf L is generated by global sections iff it is base-point-free, i.e., the global sections have no common zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base points/base locus definitions: points where all global sections vanish; scheme-theoretic base locus is the scheme-theoretic intersection of vanishing loci. The base-point-free locus is open. Tensor product of base-point-free line bundles is base-point-free (Exercise 16.1.B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear series and complete linear series (|L|)
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear series is a finite-dimensional k-vector space V together with a map V → Γ(X, L); if this map is an isomorphism it is the complete linear series |L|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notions of base points, base-point-free, and induced maps to projective space apply to linear series as well. Choosing a basis of an (n+1)-dimensional base-point-free linear series gives a morphism to Pn_k (Exercise 15.2.A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence: morphisms X → Pn ↔ (L, s0,...,sn) up to isomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 15.2.2: Morphisms X → Pn are in bijection with data (L, s0,...,sn) where L is an invertible sheaf and s0,...,sn are sections with no common zeros, modulo isomorphism of these data (and multiplication by global units).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction from sections to morphism: trivialize L locally and use coordinates to construct the map (Exercise 15.2.A). Conversely, pull back O(1) along a morphism to get L = π*O(1) and sections π*xi (proof sketched in text). This description works over Z or any base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition functions and isomorphism L ≅ π*O(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If s0,...,sn induce π : X → Pn, then on opens where si ≠ 0 the transition functions for L are si/sj which equal π*(xi/xj), giving an isomorphism L ≅ π*O(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the heart of the proof of Theorem 15.2.2: comparing transition functions shows the two constructions are inverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for map to be a closed embedding via sections
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Pn given by sections s0,...,sn is a closed embedding iff (i) each open X_si is affine, and (ii) for each i the ring map A[y0,...,yn] → Γ(X_si, O) sending y_j ↦ s_j/s_i is surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion (Exercise 15.2.H) provides a concrete affine-local test: on each trivializing affine patch the coordinate ring is generated by the ratios s_j/s_i; surjectivity yields that the map is a closed immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veronese embedding and use of O(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete linear series |O(d)| on Pn gives the Veronese embedding ν_d : Pn → P^N (N = (n+d choose n ) − 1) because sections of O(d) correspond to degree-d homogeneous polynomials and have no common zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dimension/count of monomials; for n=1 this gives rational normal curves. Exercise 15.2.I relates degree of map P1 → Pn to d and degeneracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of a map P1 → Pn via pullback of hyperplane (intersection multiplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: For π : P1 → Pn corresponding to O(d), intersecting with a general hyperplane H (pullback π*H as a section of OP1(d)) yields exactly d zeros counted with multiplicity; this gives the classical degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interprets degree as number of intersection points (with multiplicity) with a general hyperplane (Exercise 15.2.L). One must define multiplicity appropriately (zeros of a section).

rubrics_metrics.name: Segre embedding and box-tensor of invertible sheaves
rubrics_metrics.description: For X × Y, the invertible sheaf OPm(a) ⊠ OPn(b) corresponds to OP^{mn+m+n}(a,b) and the complete linear series of OP(1,1) gives the Segre embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If φ_L : X → P^r and φ_M : X → P^s arise from base-point-free linear series on L and M, then composing with the Segre embedding gives a morphism corresponding to the base-point-free series of L ⊗ M (box/Segre formalism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automorphisms of projective space ↔ PGL(n+1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Automorphisms Aut(Pn_k) (over a field k) correspond to invertible linear maps on Γ(Pn, O(1)), i.e., PGL_{n+1}(k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 15.2.D: π* induces an isomorphism on Γ(Pn, O(1)); matrices modulo scalars give projective transformations. Over arbitrary base rings subtleties arise (see remark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonexistence of nonconstant maps from Pn to smaller-dimension quasi-projective varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is quasiprojective and π : Pn_k → X is a morphism, then either the image has dimension n or π contracts Pn_k to a point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idea: reduce to algebraically closed infinite field, compute d via π*OPn(1) ≅ OPn(d) and argue d = 0 by intersecting hypersurfaces (Exercise 15.2.M).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gluing closed subschemes can produce proper but nonprojective varieties (obstruction via degree mismatch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gluing two projective pieces along isomorphic closed subschemes can yield a proper scheme that is not projective: restricting a hypothetical ample/invertible sheaf to components yields contradictory degree relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction (15.2.13): glue X1 and X2 along specified lines/conics so that degree constraints (n1 = 2n2 and 2n1 = n2) contradict, showing no global ample L can exist. This is an example showing projectivity has additional global constraints beyond properness.
